nodes.label: P-Waves (Primary)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fastest seismic waves, first to arrive at seismograph. Longitudinal compressional waves where particles vibrate parallel to direction of propagation. Can travel through solids, liquids, and gases. Speed increases with density and rigidity of medium. Used to infer earth's interior structure.

nodes.label: S-Waves (Secondary)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Transverse shear waves where particles vibrate perpendicular to direction of propagation. Slower than P-waves. Cannot travel through liquids, creating a shadow zone. Their inability to pass through the outer core proved it is liquid. Critical evidence for earth's interior layering.

nodes.label: Surface Waves (L-Waves)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Seismic waves that travel along the earth's surface. Most destructive, cause maximum damage during earthquakes. Include Rayleigh waves (rolling motion) and Love waves (horizontal shaking). Travel slower than body waves but with greater amplitude.

nodes.label: Shadow Zone
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Region on earth's surface where no seismic waves are detected after an earthquake. P-wave shadow zone exists between 104-140 degrees from epicenter due to refraction by liquid outer core. S-wave shadow zone exists beyond 104 degrees as S-waves cannot pass through liquid core.

nodes.label: Mercalli Scale
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Scale measuring earthquake intensity based on observed effects on people, structures, and natural features. Ranges from I (not felt) to XII (total destruction). Intensity varies with distance from epicenter, local geology, and building quality. Contrasted with Richter scale which measures magnitude.

nodes.label: Lithosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rigid outermost shell of the earth comprising the crust and uppermost solid mantle. About 100 km thick. Broken into tectonic plates that float on the asthenosphere. Continental lithosphere is thicker than oceanic lithosphere. The concept is fundamental to plate tectonics theory.

nodes.label: Asthenosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Zone within the upper mantle from about 100-410 km depth. Partially molten, weak, and plastic (ductile). Convection currents in this layer drive plate tectonic movements. Source of magma that feeds volcanoes. Lithospheric plates float and move on this layer.

nodes.label: Stratosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Second layer from 18 to 50 km altitude. Temperature increases with altitude due to absorption of UV radiation by the ozone layer. Virtually no weather, very dry. Ideal for jet aircraft flying. Contains the ozone layer (20-35 km). Temperature inversion makes it very stable.

nodes.label: Mesosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Third layer from 50 to 80 km altitude. Temperature decreases with altitude, reaching the coldest temperatures in the atmosphere (about -90C) at the mesopause. Meteors burn up in this layer due to friction. Noctilucent clouds (highest clouds) may form near the mesopause.

nodes.label: Thermosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fourth layer from 80 to 700 km altitude. Temperature increases rapidly with altitude due to absorption of high-energy solar radiation, reaching over 1000C. Despite high temperature, would not feel hot due to extremely low air density. Contains the ionosphere (80-400 km) where radio waves are reflected.

nodes.label: Exosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Outermost layer of the atmosphere beyond 700 km. Extremely thin with molecules widely dispersed. Gradually merges into outer space. Hydrogen and helium are the main gases. Satellites orbit in this zone. Gas molecules can escape earth's gravity from this layer.

nodes.label: Ozone Layer
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Concentration of ozone (O3) in the stratosphere at 20-35 km altitude. Absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun, protecting life on earth. Ozone depletion caused by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) leads to ozone holes, especially over Antarctica. Montreal Protocol (1987) banned ozone-depleting substances.

nodes.label: Ionosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Ionized region within the thermosphere (80-400 km) containing electrically charged particles. Formed by ionization of gases by solar radiation. Reflects radio waves back to earth's surface, enabling long-distance radio communication. Aurora borealis and aurora australis occur here. Has multiple layers (D, E, F).

nodes.label: Oxygen
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Second most abundant atmospheric gas at 20.95%. Essential for respiration of all aerobic organisms and combustion. Produced by photosynthesis. Absent from early earth's atmosphere; appeared about 2.5 billion years ago (Great Oxygenation Event). Decreases with altitude. Forms ozone (O3) in the stratosphere.

nodes.label: Temperature Inversion
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Abnormal condition where temperature increases with altitude instead of decreasing. Occurs in the stratosphere normally, and in the troposphere under specific conditions (clear nights, valleys, anticyclonic conditions). Traps air pollutants near the surface causing smog. Common in valleys and basins during winter.

nodes.label: Aurora
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Natural light display in the sky predominantly seen in high-latitude regions. Aurora borealis (northern lights) and aurora australis (southern lights). Caused by charged particles from solar wind interacting with atmospheric gases in the ionosphere/thermosphere. Oxygen produces green/red, nitrogen produces blue/purple colours.

nodes.label: Ozone Depletion
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer caused by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other ozone-depleting substances. Ozone hole discovered over Antarctica in 1985. CFCs release chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone molecules. Increases harmful UV-B radiation reaching surface, causing skin cancer and crop damage.

nodes.label: Gulf Stream
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Powerful warm ocean current in the North Atlantic flowing from Gulf of Mexico along the eastern coast of North America and across the Atlantic. Continues as the North Atlantic Drift toward western Europe. Moderates climate of western Europe making it much warmer than same latitudes in North America. About 80 km wide and 1000m deep.

nodes.label: Tides
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Periodic rise and fall of sea level caused by gravitational pull of the moon and sun. Semi-diurnal (two high, two low per day) is most common. Spring tides (higher) occur during full and new moon when sun and moon align. Neap tides (lower) during quarter moons. Tidal range varies greatly by location.

nodes.label: Spring Tide
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Tides with maximum tidal range occurring during full moon and new moon when the sun, moon, and earth are in alignment (syzygy). Gravitational forces of sun and moon combine, creating higher high tides and lower low tides. Not related to the season of spring. Occurs roughly every two weeks.

nodes.label: Neap Tide
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Tides with minimum tidal range occurring during first and third quarter moons when sun and moon are at right angles (quadrature) relative to earth. Gravitational forces partially cancel each other, producing moderate tides. Tidal range is typically 30-40% less than spring tides.

nodes.label: Tidal Energy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Renewable energy generated by harnessing the kinetic energy of tidal movements. Requires large tidal range (minimum 5m). Tidal barrages capture water at high tide and release through turbines. India's Gulf of Khambhat has among the highest tidal ranges. Clean energy but limited suitable locations and high infrastructure costs.

nodes.label: Biosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Narrow zone of earth where lithosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere interact to support life. Extends from deep ocean floors to about 10 km altitude. Contains all living organisms and their physical environment. Term coined by Eduard Suess. Functions as a self-regulating system cycling matter and energy.

nodes.label: Ecosystem
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Functional unit of nature comprising all living organisms (biotic) and their physical environment (abiotic) interacting as a system. Energy flows in one direction (sun to producers to consumers to decomposers), matter cycles. Types: terrestrial (forests, grasslands, deserts) and aquatic (freshwater, marine). Term coined by Arthur Tansley.

nodes.label: Food Chain and Food Web
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Food chain is a linear sequence of energy transfer from producers to consumers. Trophic levels: producers (plants), primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores), tertiary consumers (top predators), decomposers. Only 10% of energy transfers between levels. Food web is the interconnected network of multiple food chains in an ecosystem.

nodes.label: Ecological Succession
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Gradual process of change in species composition of an ecological community over time. Primary succession occurs on bare surfaces (volcanic rock, sand dunes) starting with pioneer species. Secondary succession occurs after disturbance (fire, flood) on existing soil. Progresses toward a climax community in equilibrium with climate.

nodes.label: Nutrient Cycling
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Movement and recycling of nutrients through the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem. Major cycles: carbon cycle, nitrogen cycle, phosphorus cycle, water cycle. Nutrients cycle between organisms, soil, water, and atmosphere. Decomposers play a critical role by breaking down dead matter and returning nutrients to the soil.

nodes.label: Carbon Cycle
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Biogeochemical cycle by which carbon is exchanged between the biosphere, lithosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere. Plants absorb CO2 through photosynthesis; released through respiration, decomposition, and combustion. Fossil fuels are stored carbon. Oceans absorb about 30% of CO2. Human activities have disrupted the cycle causing excess atmospheric CO2.

nodes.label: Nitrogen Cycle
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Biogeochemical cycle converting atmospheric nitrogen (N2) into biologically usable forms and back. Steps: nitrogen fixation (by bacteria, lightning), nitrification, assimilation by plants, ammonification (decomposition), and denitrification (return to atmosphere). Rhizobium bacteria fix nitrogen in legume root nodules. Excess fertilizer causes eutrophication.

nodes.label: Ecology
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Scientific study of interactions between organisms and their environment. Coined by Ernst Haeckel. Levels of organization: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome, biosphere. Studies energy flow, nutrient cycling, population dynamics, species interactions (competition, predation, symbiosis), and community structure.

nodes.label: Photosynthesis
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Process by which green plants convert solar energy, CO2, and water into glucose and oxygen using chlorophyll. Foundation of nearly all food chains on earth. Occurs primarily in leaves. Responsible for producing atmospheric oxygen. Rate depends on light, temperature, CO2 concentration, and water availability.

nodes.label: Ecosystem Diversity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Variety of ecosystems in a region. India has diverse ecosystems from coral reefs to alpine meadows, mangroves to deserts, rainforests to temperate forests. Greater ecosystem diversity supports more species and provides varied ecological services. Loss of any ecosystem reduces overall biodiversity.

nodes.label: Endangered Species
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Species facing high risk of extinction. IUCN Red List categories: Extinct, Extinct in Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern. India's endangered species include Bengal tiger, Asiatic lion, Indian rhinoceros, snow leopard, Gangetic dolphin. Protected under Wildlife Protection Act 1972.

nodes.label: IUCN Red List
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: International Union for Conservation of Nature maintains the most comprehensive inventory of conservation status of species. Red List categorizes species by extinction risk. Founded in 1948. Headquartered in Gland, Switzerland. Provides scientific basis for conservation action. Over 150,000 species assessed.

nodes.label: In-situ Conservation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Conservation of species in their natural habitats. Most effective long-term strategy. Includes national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves, and community reserves. India has 106 national parks, 567 wildlife sanctuaries, and 18 biosphere reserves. Protects entire ecosystems and ecological processes.

nodes.label: Biosphere Reserve
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Large area designated under UNESCO's Man and Biosphere Programme for conservation with sustainable use. Three zones: core (strictly protected), buffer (limited human activity), and transition (sustainable development). India has 18 biosphere reserves, 12 in UNESCO World Network. Includes Nilgiri (first in India, 1986), Sundarbans, Gulf of Mannar.

nodes.label: Wildlife Sanctuary
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Protected area primarily for conservation of wildlife. Some human activities like grazing may be allowed with permission unlike national parks. Boundaries can be altered. India has 567+ wildlife sanctuaries. Can be upgraded to national parks. Examples: Periyar, Bharatpur (Keoladeo), Mudumalai, Chilika.

nodes.label: Threats to Biodiversity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Major threats: habitat destruction and fragmentation (deforestation, urbanization), overexploitation (hunting, overfishing), invasive alien species, pollution, and climate change. Habitat loss is the single greatest threat. Current rate of extinction is 100-1000 times the natural background rate. Sixth mass extinction is underway according to scientists.

nodes.label: CITES
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (1975). Regulates international trade in specimens of wild animals and plants. Three appendices: I (complete trade ban, e.g., tiger, elephant), II (regulated trade), III (protected in at least one country). 184 member parties.

nodes.label: Ramsar Convention
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: International treaty for conservation and sustainable use of wetlands (1971). Ramsar Sites are wetlands of international importance. India has 80+ Ramsar Sites including Chilika Lake, Keoladeo (Bharatpur), Loktak Lake, Wular Lake, and Sundarbans. Wetlands provide critical ecosystem services: water filtration, flood control, biodiversity habitat.

nodes.label: India - Location and Extent
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India lies entirely in the Northern and Eastern Hemispheres. Extends from 8d4'N to 37d6'N latitude and 68d7'E to 97d25'E longitude. Total area: 3.28 million sq km (7th largest country). Tropic of Cancer (23.5N) divides India roughly in half. The 82d30'E meridian is Indian Standard Time (IST) passing through Mirzapur.

nodes.label: India's Neighbouring Countries
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India shares land borders with 7 countries: Pakistan and Afghanistan (NW), China, Nepal, Bhutan (N), Myanmar and Bangladesh (E). Maritime neighbours across sea: Sri Lanka (separated by Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar) and Maldives (SW in Arabian Sea). India's central location in Indian Ocean gives strategic advantage for trade.

nodes.label: Indian Standard Time (IST)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Standard time for India based on the 82d30'E meridian passing through Mirzapur (near Allahabad/Prayagraj), Uttar Pradesh. IST is UTC+5:30. Despite India's east-west extent spanning about 30 degrees of longitude (2 hours of time difference), a single time zone is used. Arunachal Pradesh sees sunrise nearly 2 hours before Gujarat.

nodes.label: Tropic of Cancer through India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: The Tropic of Cancer (23d30'N) passes through 8 Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, and Mizoram. Divides India into tropical (south) and subtropical (north) zones. Affects climate patterns, vegetation, and agricultural practices. Sun is directly overhead on June 21 (summer solstice).

nodes.label: States and Union Territories
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India has 28 states and 8 Union Territories. Rajasthan is the largest state by area, Goa the smallest. UP is the most populous. UTs include Delhi (NCT), Chandigarh, Puducherry, Ladakh, J&K, Dadra and Nagar Haveli & Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

nodes.label: Andaman and Nicobar Islands
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Archipelago of 572 islands in the Bay of Bengal. India's southernmost point (Indira Point/Pygmalion Point on Great Nicobar Island, 6d45'N). Separated by the Ten Degree Channel (Andaman and Nicobar groups). Volcanic activity: Barren Island (only active volcano in India). Rich biodiversity, dense tropical forests. Capital: Port Blair.

nodes.label: Lakshadweep Islands
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Group of 36 coral islands (atolls) in the Arabian Sea off the Kerala coast. India's smallest Union Territory. Capital: Kavaratti. Formed by coral reef formation on submerged volcanic peaks. Only coral islands of India. Separated from Maldives by Eight Degree Channel. Total area only 32 sq km.

nodes.label: Palk Strait
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Narrow strait between southeastern India (Tamil Nadu) and northwestern Sri Lanka. About 53-80 km wide. Contains Pamban Island (Rameswaram). Adam's Bridge (Ram Setu) is a chain of limestone shoals connecting India and Sri Lanka across the strait. Shallow waters with rich marine biodiversity.

nodes.label: India's Area and Dimensions
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Total area: 3.28 million sq km (2.4% of world's total area). North-south extent: 3,214 km from Kashmir to Kanyakumari. East-west extent: 2,933 km from Arunachal Pradesh to Gujarat. Land boundary: 15,200 km. Seventh largest country after Russia, Canada, USA, China, Brazil, and Australia.

nodes.label: India's Land Boundaries
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Total land boundary: about 15,200 km. Bangladesh shares longest border (4,096 km). China: 3,488 km. Pakistan: 3,323 km. Nepal: 1,751 km. Myanmar: 1,643 km. Bhutan: 699 km. Afghanistan: 106 km (LoC area via PoK). Major boundary disputes exist with China (LAC) and Pakistan (LoC in J&K, Sir Creek, Siachen).

nodes.label: Northern Plains (Indo-Gangetic Plains)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Vast alluvial plain formed by deposition of rivers flowing from Himalayas. Extends about 2,400 km east-west, 240-320 km wide. One of the world's most extensive and fertile plains. Divisions: Bhabar (pebble zone at foothills), Terai (marshy), Bhangar (older alluvium), Khadar (newer alluvium, floodplains). Supports India's densest population.

nodes.label: Bhabar
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Narrow belt of pebble-studded deposits along the Himalayan foothills, 8-16 km wide. Formed by merging of alluvial fans. Streams disappear underground in this porous zone. Not suitable for agriculture due to porosity. Lies between the Shiwaliks and the Terai. Rivers re-emerge in the Terai zone.

nodes.label: Terai
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Marshy, swampy belt south of Bhabar where underground streams re-emerge. Originally dense forests with wildlife, now largely cleared for agriculture. Fertile agricultural land. Found along the southern Himalayan foothills from Punjab to Assam. Important for rice cultivation and sugarcane farming.

nodes.label: Peninsular Plateau
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Oldest and most stable landmass of India, part of ancient Gondwana. Composed of igneous and metamorphic rocks. Triangular shape. General elevation 600-900m. Two divisions: Central Highlands (north of Narmada) and Deccan Plateau (south of Narmada). Bounded by Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats. Rich in minerals.

nodes.label: Central Highlands
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Northern part of Peninsular Plateau north of Narmada River. Includes Malwa Plateau, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand, and Chotanagpur Plateau. Wider in the west, narrows eastward. Chambal, Betwa, Ken rivers flow northward to join Yamuna. Aravalli Range on the northwestern edge is one of the world's oldest fold mountains.

nodes.label: Deccan Plateau
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Triangular plateau south of Narmada River. Higher in the west (Western Ghats) and slopes gently eastward. Major rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) flow west to east. Composed largely of Deccan Trap basalt in the northwestern part. Black (regur) soil derived from basalt. Major mineral deposits. Includes Deccan Trap, Telangana Plateau.

nodes.label: Western Ghats (Sahyadri)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Continuous mountain range along the western coast from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu, about 1,600 km. Average elevation 900-1600m. Higher than Eastern Ghats. Major peaks: Anai Mudi (2,695m, highest in South India), Doda Betta. UNESCO World Heritage Site. Biodiversity hotspot. Causes orographic rainfall on windward side. Source of major peninsular rivers.

nodes.label: Eastern Ghats
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Discontinuous hill ranges along the eastern coast from Odisha to Tamil Nadu. Dissected by major east-flowing rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi). Lower and more irregular than Western Ghats. Highest peak: Mahendragiri (1,501m). Merge with Western Ghats at Nilgiri Hills in the south.

nodes.label: Aravalli Range
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: One of the world's oldest fold mountains running NE-SW for about 800 km from Delhi to Palanpur (Gujarat). Remnant of ancient mountains (Precambrian). Heavily eroded and lowered. Highest peak: Guru Shikhar (1,722m) on Mt Abu. Divides Rajasthan into eastern fertile and western arid parts. Rich in minerals (marble, mica).

nodes.label: Narmada and Tapi Rift Valleys
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Two major westward-flowing rivers of peninsular India flowing through rift valleys (fault-controlled). Narmada flows between Vindhya Range (north) and Satpura Range (south). Tapi flows south of Satpura Range. Both form estuaries (not deltas) at their mouths. Their valleys divide the Peninsular Plateau from the Central Highlands.

nodes.label: Deccan Traps
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Massive basaltic lava flow covering about 500,000 sq km of western and central India. Formed about 66 million years ago during massive volcanic eruptions (possibly linked to Chicxulub asteroid impact and dinosaur extinction). Weathering of basalt produces fertile black cotton soil (regur). Step-like topography (trap means 'step' in Swedish).

nodes.label: Nilgiri Hills
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Mountain range at the junction of Western and Eastern Ghats in Tamil Nadu-Kerala-Karnataka tri-junction. Includes Doda Betta (2,637m). Site of Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (first in India, 1986). Home to indigenous Toda people. Ooty (Udhagamandalam) is a famous hill station. Important biodiversity area.

nodes.label: Vindhya and Satpura Ranges
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Two parallel mountain ranges in central India. Vindhya Range runs east-west, traditionally considered the divide between North and South India. Satpura Range runs parallel to the south between Narmada and Tapi rivers. Highest peak: Dhupgarh (1,350m) in Satpura. Both are block mountains formed by faulting.

nodes.label: Thar Desert (Great Indian Desert)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Largest desert in India located in western Rajasthan, extending into Pakistan (Cholistan/Thal). Bounded by Aravalli Range on the east. Covers about 200,000 sq km. Features sand dunes, rocky surfaces, salt lakes (Sambhar, Didwana). Luni is the only river. Indira Gandhi Canal brings water from Sutlej. Extreme temperatures and low rainfall (<150mm).

nodes.label: Indian Coastal Plains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Narrow plains along India's peninsular coast. Western coast: narrower, includes Konkan (Maharashtra), Malabar (Kerala), and Kanara (Karnataka) coasts. Eastern coast: wider, includes Coromandel (TN-AP), Northern Circars (AP-Odisha). Eastern coast has more deltas due to eastward flowing rivers. Both have distinct features and ports.

nodes.label: Anai Mudi
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Highest peak of the Western Ghats and South India at 2,695m, located in Anaimalai Hills of Kerala. Part of the Eravikulam National Park. The convergence point of Anaimalai Hills, Palani Hills, and Cardamom Hills. Important for Nilgiri tahr conservation. Higher than any peak in the Eastern Ghats.

nodes.label: India's Drainage System
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India's rivers classified by drainage into Bay of Bengal (east-flowing, 77% of drainage area) and Arabian Sea (west-flowing). Also classified by origin: Himalayan (perennial, snow-fed + rain-fed) and Peninsular (seasonal, rain-fed only). Major drainage patterns: dendritic, trellis, rectangular, radial.

nodes.label: Himalayan Rivers
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rivers originating from the Himalayas. Perennial as they are fed by both rainfall and snowmelt/glaciers. Long courses with large basins. Three major systems: Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra. All are antecedent rivers (older than the Himalayas) that cut deep gorges through the mountains. Carry heavy sediment load.

nodes.label: Peninsular Rivers
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rivers originating from the Peninsular Plateau. Mostly seasonal and rain-fed with fluctuating flow. Shorter courses, shallower valleys. Most flow eastward into Bay of Bengal (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi). Exceptions flowing westward: Narmada and Tapi (through rift valleys). Fixed courses in hard rock terrain.

nodes.label: Ganga River System
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Most important river system of India. Originates as Bhagirathi from Gangotri Glacier (Uttarakhand). Joins Alaknanda at Devprayag to form Ganga. Total length: 2,525 km. Major tributaries: Yamuna (right), Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi (left), Son, Chambal (right). Forms world's largest delta (Sundarbans) with Brahmaputra. Basin covers 26% of India.

nodes.label: Brahmaputra River System
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Major river originating as Tsangpo near Mansarovar (Tibet) at 5,150m. Enters India through Arunachal Pradesh as Dihang. Length: 2,900 km (916 km in India). Known by different names: Tsangpo (Tibet), Dihang/Brahmaputra (India), Jamuna (Bangladesh). Forms massive braided river in Assam. Highly flood-prone. Merges with Ganga in Bangladesh.

nodes.label: Indus River System
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: One of the longest rivers in Asia (2,880 km), originating near Mansarovar Lake (Tibet). Enters India through Ladakh. Major tributaries: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej (Punjab rivers, all left bank). Most of its course is in Pakistan. Indus Waters Treaty (1960) allocates waters between India and Pakistan. Ancient Indus Valley civilization developed here.

nodes.label: Godavari River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Largest peninsular river, called 'Dakshin Ganga' (Ganga of the South). Originates at Trimbakeshwar near Nasik (Maharashtra). Length: 1,465 km. Drains parts of Maharashtra, Telangana, AP, Chhattisgarh, and Odisha. Major tributaries: Pranhita, Indravati, Manjira, Purna. Forms a large delta on the AP coast. Flows eastward into Bay of Bengal.

nodes.label: Krishna River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Second largest peninsular river. Originates near Mahabaleshwar (Maharashtra). Length: 1,401 km. Flows through Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, and AP. Major tributaries: Tungabhadra, Bhima, Koyna, Musi. Forms a large delta in AP. Major dams: Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam, Almatti. Interstate water disputes between states.

nodes.label: Kaveri (Cauvery) River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Sacred river of South India. Originates at Talakaveri in Brahmagiri Hills (Coorg, Karnataka). Length: 800 km. Flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Major tributaries: Hemavati, Kabini, Bhavani, Amaravati. Forms Shivasamudram Falls and a fertile delta in Tamil Nadu. Subject of long-running interstate water dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

nodes.label: Narmada River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Longest west-flowing peninsular river. Originates from Amarkantak Plateau (MP). Length: 1,312 km. Flows through a rift valley between Vindhya and Satpura ranges. Forms an estuary (not delta) at Gulf of Khambhat. Dhuandhar Falls near Jabalpur. Sardar Sarovar Dam is the major project. Does not form a delta due to rift valley course.

nodes.label: Mahanadi River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rises in Sihawa hills of Chhattisgarh. Length: 851 km. Flows through Chhattisgarh and Odisha. Major tributaries: Seonath, Hasdeo, Mand, Ib, Jonk, Tel. Forms a large delta near Cuttack. Hirakud Dam (one of the longest earthen dams) built across it. Historically called 'sorrow of Odisha' due to floods.

nodes.label: Tapi (Tapti) River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: West-flowing river originating in Betul district (MP) near Satpura Range. Length: 724 km. Flows through MP, Maharashtra, and Gujarat. Runs parallel to Narmada but south of the Satpura Range. Forms estuary at Gulf of Khambhat near Surat. Ukai Dam is the major project. Second longest west-flowing peninsular river.

nodes.label: Yamuna River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Longest tributary of the Ganga. Originates from Yamunotri Glacier on Bandarpunch Peak (Uttarakhand). Length: 1,376 km. Major tributaries: Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken (right bank from peninsular region). Flows through Delhi, one of the most polluted stretches. Meets Ganga at Triveni Sangam (Prayagraj). Parallel to Ganga for most of its course.

nodes.label: Chambal River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Tributary of Yamuna originating near Mhow (MP). Flows through MP, Rajasthan and along the MP-UP border. Length: 960 km. Known for deep ravines and badlands along its course. Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar, and Jawahar Sagar dams form a cascade. Relatively unpolluted due to ravine terrain limiting settlement.

nodes.label: Sundarbans Delta
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: World's largest delta formed by Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna system. Covers about 40,000 sq km in India and Bangladesh. World's largest mangrove forest. UNESCO World Heritage Site. Home to the Royal Bengal Tiger. Highly vulnerable to sea-level rise and cyclones. Named after Sundari trees (Heritiera littoralis).

nodes.label: Lakes of India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India has diverse lakes formed by various processes. Freshwater: Wular (largest freshwater, J&K), Dal, Bhimtal, Nainital (tectonic/glacial). Saltwater: Chilika (largest coastal lagoon, Odisha), Sambhar (Rajasthan, salt production), Pulicat. Crater lake: Lonar (Maharashtra). Man-made: Gobind Sagar, Nagarjuna Sagar. Many are Ramsar Sites.

nodes.label: Indus Waters Treaty
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Treaty signed in 1960 between India and Pakistan, brokered by the World Bank. Allocates waters of the Indus system: India gets eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej), Pakistan gets western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab). India can use western rivers for limited non-consumptive purposes. One of the most durable water-sharing treaties globally.

nodes.label: Antecedent Rivers
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rivers older than the landform they cut through. Himalayan rivers like Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra existed before the Himalayas rose and cut deep gorges through the rising mountains. Evidence: transverse courses cutting across mountain ranges. The rivers maintained their course as the mountains slowly uplifted around them.

nodes.label: River Rejuvenation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Renewal of erosive activity by a river due to uplift of land or fall in base level. Creates features like river terraces, incised meanders, knick points, and rejuvenated valleys. Peninsular rivers show evidence of rejuvenation through waterfalls and rapids. Indicates tectonic uplift of the Peninsular Plateau.

nodes.label: Watershed/Drainage Divide
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Elevated area separating two adjacent drainage basins. The Western Ghats serve as the major watershed of peninsular India, separating west-flowing and east-flowing rivers. Himalayas form the watershed between Indian and central Asian drainage. Watershed management is critical for water conservation and flood control.

nodes.label: Sutlej River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Longest of the five Punjab rivers. Originates near Mansarovar Lake (Tibet) at Rakas Tal. Enters India through Shipki La pass in Himachal Pradesh. Length: 1,450 km. Bhakra-Nangal Dam built on it. Feeds the Indira Gandhi Canal (longest canal in India) for irrigation in Rajasthan. Allocated to India under Indus Waters Treaty.

nodes.label: Tropical Evergreen Forest
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Found in areas with >200cm rainfall and temperatures above 22C year-round. Dense, multi-layered canopy, no definite growing season. Trees don't shed leaves simultaneously. Found in Western Ghats, northeastern India, Andaman Islands. Species: rosewood, ebony, mahogany, rubber, bamboo. Difficult to exploit commercially due to density and diversity.

nodes.label: Tropical Deciduous Forest
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Most widespread vegetation in India. Trees shed leaves in dry season to conserve moisture. Two subtypes: moist deciduous (100-200cm rainfall; teak, sal, shisham, mahua, bamboo) and dry deciduous (70-100cm rainfall; more open, thorn-like). Found across central India, eastern slopes of Western Ghats, NE states. Most commercially important.

nodes.label: Tropical Thorn and Scrub Forest
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Found in areas receiving less than 70cm rainfall. Semi-arid to arid regions of Rajasthan, Gujarat, MP, UP. Trees are stunted with thorns, thick bark, waxy leaves, deep roots. Species: babool (acacia), ber (jujube), wild date palm, khair, neem. Cacti and euphorbias common. Adapted to drought and high temperatures.

nodes.label: Mangrove Forest
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Salt-tolerant forests in tidal/coastal areas and river deltas. Sundarbans (largest mangrove forest in the world). Other areas: Bhitarkanika (Odisha), Pichavaram (TN), Gulf of Kutch, Andaman islands. Species: Rhizophora, Avicennia, Sundari. Adaptations: stilt roots, pneumatophores (breathing roots), viviparous germination. Critical for coastal protection.

nodes.label: Teak (Sagwan)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Most important timber tree of India. Found in tropical moist and dry deciduous forests. Grows best in 100-200cm rainfall areas. Major teak forests in MP, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat, Rajasthan. Highly durable, termite-resistant wood used for furniture and shipbuilding. India is the largest producer and consumer of teak globally.

nodes.label: Sal
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Important timber tree of northern and central India. Dominant in moist and dry deciduous forests of UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Assam. Produces hard, durable wood used in construction and railway sleepers. Along with teak, forms the backbone of India's timber industry. Prefers alluvial soil and moderate rainfall.

nodes.label: Deforestation in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Major causes: agriculture expansion, logging, mining, urbanization, infrastructure projects, and shifting cultivation (jhum) in northeast. India lost significant forest cover historically; now showing slow increase. Forest Survey of India conducts biennial assessment. Chipko Movement (1973) and Appiko Movement (1983) are landmark conservation movements.

nodes.label: Moist Deciduous Forest
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Found in areas receiving 100-200cm rainfall. Transitional between tropical evergreen and dry deciduous. Shed leaves for 6-8 weeks during dry season. Found along eastern slopes of Western Ghats, NE India, foothills of Himalayas, Jharkhand, Odisha. Species: teak, sal, shisham, hurra, mahua, amla, bamboo. Most commercially exploited forests.

nodes.label: Dry Deciduous Forest
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Found in areas receiving 70-100cm rainfall. Trees shed leaves for long dry period. More open canopy than moist deciduous. Found in central and western India, rain shadow areas. Species: teak, sal, peepal, neem, babool. Gradually transitions into thorn forest with decreasing rainfall. Covers large areas of MP, Maharashtra, UP.

nodes.label: India's Wildlife
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India has about 91,000 animal species. Mega-fauna includes Bengal tiger, Asiatic lion (Gir only), Indian elephant, one-horned rhinoceros (Kaziranga), snow leopard. India has 3 of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots. Wildlife Protection Act 1972 provides legal framework. Project Tiger (1973) and Project Elephant (1992) are major conservation programs.

nodes.label: Soils of India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India has diverse soil types due to varied climate, topography, parent rock, and vegetation. Major types: alluvial, black (regur), red, laterite, arid/desert, forest/mountain, peaty/marshy, and saline/alkaline. Soil is a renewable resource but forms very slowly (1 cm in 1000 years). ICAR classifies Indian soils into 8 major types.

nodes.label: Red Soil
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Formed by weathering of ancient crystalline and metamorphic rocks (granite, gneiss). Red color due to iron oxide content. Found in southern and eastern parts of Deccan Plateau, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, and parts of northeastern states. Generally poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus but responds well to fertilizers. Porous and friable.

nodes.label: Peaty/Marshy Soil
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Found in areas of heavy rainfall and high humidity with waterlogged conditions. Rich in organic matter (humus) but very acidic. Black in color, heavy, and poorly aerated. Found in Kerala (kuttanad), northern Bihar, Sundarbans, coastal Odisha. Below sea level in some Kerala regions. Suitable for rice cultivation when drained.

nodes.label: Saline/Alkaline Soil (Usar/Reh)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Soil with high salt concentration due to poor drainage, high evaporation, or waterlogging. Also called Reh, Usar, Kallar. Found in arid and semi-arid regions (Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, UP) and coastal areas. White crust of salt on surface. Unfit for cultivation without reclamation. Remedied by gypsum application and proper drainage.

nodes.label: Bhangar (Old Alluvium)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Older alluvial soil found above the flood plains of rivers. Contains calcium carbonate nodules called kankar. Less fertile than Khadar. Forms terraces above the present river level. More compact and darker in color. Found in the upper reaches of the northern plains away from active flood areas.

nodes.label: Khadar (New Alluvium)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Newer alluvial soil deposited in river floodplains, renewed with each flood. More fertile than Bhangar as it receives fresh deposits of silt annually. Light in color and sandy-loamy in texture. Found in the immediate vicinity of rivers. Supports intensive agriculture. Risk of flooding makes settlement challenging.

nodes.label: Leaching
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Washing away of soluble soil nutrients by percolating rainwater. Most intense in areas of heavy rainfall. Responsible for formation of laterite soils where silica is leached leaving iron/aluminium oxides. Makes tropical soils acidic and nutrient-poor. Contrasted with capillary action in dry areas which brings salts to the surface.

nodes.label: Rural-Urban Composition
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: About 72% of India's population lives in villages (2001). Bihar and Sikkim have very high rural percentage. Urban population is 27.8% showing faster growth since 1931. Rural-urban migration drives urban growth.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Population Doubling Time
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Time taken for population to double at current annual growth rate. At India's 2.4% annual growth rate, population estimated to double in 36 years and potentially surpass China.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Language Families of India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Four families: Indo-European/Aryan (73%) in north; Dravidian (20%) in south; Austric/Nishada (1.38%) in tribal central-east and Meghalaya; Sino-Tibetan/Kirata (0.85%) in northeast hills.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Streams of Migration
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Four streams: Rural-Rural, Rural-Urban, Urban-Urban, Urban-Rural. Females dominate R-R (marriage). Males dominate R-U (employment). 81 million intra-state out of 98 million total migrants.

nodes.label: Push and Pull Factors
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Push: poverty, land pressure, lack of infrastructure, natural disasters. Pull: better employment, higher wages, education, health. Work/employment main cause for male migration (38%), marriage for female (65%).

nodes.label: Marriage Migration
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: About 65% of female migration in India due to marriage. Most important cause in rural areas. Exception: Meghalaya (matrilineal society) where reverse pattern exists.

nodes.label: Brain Drain
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Loss of highly skilled professionals from developing to developed countries. Market for advanced skills has become global. Dynamic economies recruit trained professionals from poor regions.

nodes.label: Green Revolution and Migration Link
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Migration from rural eastern UP, Bihar, MP and Orissa to Punjab, Haryana, western UP provided labour essential for green revolution agricultural development success.

nodes.label: Net Migration by State
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Maharashtra highest net in-migration (2.3M), followed by Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana. UP largest net out-migration (-2.6M), Bihar (-1.7M). Greater Mumbai received highest urban in-migrants.

nodes.label: HDI Indicators (India)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Three indicators: health (life expectancy), education (literacy), resources (per capita income). Kerala 0.638, Punjab 0.537, TN 0.531. Bihar 0.367, Assam 0.386.

nodes.label: UNDP Human Development Report
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: First published 1990. Defines human development as enlarging people's choices. Ranks all countries on HDI scores annually.

nodes.label: Health Indicators
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Death rate 25.1 to 8.1/1000 (1951-1999). IMR 148 to 70. Life expectancy 37 to 62 years. Child sex ratio alarming in Haryana/Punjab (<800).

nodes.label: Per Capita Income Disparities
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Developed states above Rs.4000/yr, poorer states below Rs.2000 (1980-81 prices). Consumption expenditure varies Rs.520-690/month.

nodes.label: Brundtland Report
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Our Common Future (1987). Along with Limits to Growth (1972), Small is Beautiful (1974), Agenda-21 (1993).

nodes.label: Rice Cultivation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Staple food. India second after China (22% world). WB, Punjab, UP, AP, TN lead. Three crops in WB: aus, aman, boro.

nodes.label: Wheat Cultivation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Second cereal. 12% world. Rabi crop in Indo-Gangetic Plain. UP, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, MP lead. High yield in Punjab/Haryana.

nodes.label: Agricultural Problems
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Erratic monsoon, low productivity, indebtedness, lack of land reforms, small holdings, lack of commercialisation, under-employment, degradation.

nodes.label: Cropping Intensity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Gross cropped area/net sown area x 100. Important for land-scarce, labour-abundant India.

nodes.label: Groundwater
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 432 cubic km replenishable. Ganga/Brahmaputra 46%. High utilisation in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, TN. Over-exploitation causes fluoride/arsenic.

nodes.label: Irrigation Demand
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Agriculture 89% surface, 92% groundwater use. Green revolution linked to irrigation. Spatio-temporal rainfall variability necessitates irrigation.

nodes.label: Water Pollution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Yamuna most polluted (Delhi-Etawah). Sabarmati, Gomti, Ganga at Kanpur/Varanasi. Water Act 1974, Environment Protection Act 1986.

nodes.label: Watershed Management
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Surface/groundwater conservation. Percolation tanks, recharge wells. Haryali, Neeru-Meeru (AP), Arvary Pani Sansad (Rajasthan). Ralegan Siddhi success.

nodes.label: National Water Policy 2002
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Priorities: drinking water, irrigation, hydro-power, navigation, industry. Regulate groundwater, monitor quality, conservation consciousness.

nodes.label: Coal
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 80% bituminous non-coking. Gondwana coalfields in Damodar Valley: Raniganj, Jharia (largest), Bokaro. Tertiary in Assam, Meghalaya. Lignite in TN.

nodes.label: Petroleum
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Sedimentary rocks. ONGC 1956. Digboi (Assam), Ankaleshwar/Mumbai High (Gujarat), Krishna-Godavari basin. 18 refineries. Liquid gold.

nodes.label: Non-Conventional Energy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Solar (Gujarat, Rajasthan), wind (50,000 MW, Lamba largest Asia), tidal (west coast), geothermal (Manikaran), bio-energy (Okhla).

nodes.label: Natural Gas
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: GAIL 1984. Found with oil. Exclusive reserves along eastern coast, Tripura, Rajasthan, offshore Gujarat/Maharashtra.

nodes.label: SAIL
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Steel Authority of India Ltd. 1973. Rourkela (German), Bhilai (Russian), Durgapur (UK). Previously HSL.

nodes.label: Planning in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Centralised through Planning Commission. Five Year Plans from 1951. Sectoral and regional planning for reducing spatial imbalances.

nodes.label: Target Area Planning
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: For backward areas: Command Area, Drought Prone, Desert, Hill Area Development. Target groups: SFDA, MFDA for small/marginal farmers.

nodes.label: Sustainable Development
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Meeting present needs without compromising future. Brundtland Report 1987. Ecological, social, economic aspects.

nodes.label: Indira Gandhi Canal
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Largest canal. Conceived 1948, launched 1958. Harike barrage, 9,060 km. Two stages, 19.63 lakh ha. Transformed Thar ecology.

nodes.label: ITDP Bharmaur
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Gaddi tribe Chamba HP. Since 1974 Fifth Plan. Female literacy 1.88% to 42.83%. Infrastructure, declined child marriage.

nodes.label: Drought Prone Programme
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fourth Plan. Employment in drought areas. Semi-arid Rajasthan, Gujarat, MP, Marathwada, Telangana, Karnataka.

nodes.label: Hill Area Development
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fifth Plan, 15 districts. Above 600m. Horticulture, plantation, animal husbandry, forestry, small industry.

nodes.label: Waterlogging and Salinity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Twin problems of intensive irrigation in Indira Gandhi Canal. Threatens long-term agricultural sustainability.

nodes.label: Agro-Climatic Planning
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 1988 by Planning Commission. Regionally balanced agriculture. Diversification: dairy, poultry, horticulture.

nodes.label: Five Year Plans
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Started 1951. First: agriculture. Second: industrialisation. Plan holidays 1966-69. Tenth 2002-07.

nodes.label: Golden Quadrilateral
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 5,846 km 4/6 lane: Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai-Kolkata. Reduces time-distance-cost. NHAI major project.

nodes.label: Communications
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Internet, radio (1923), TV (1959), Doordarshan, INSAT (1983), IRS satellites, NRSA Hyderabad, PSLV.

nodes.label: Border Roads Organisation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: May 1960. 40,450 km by 2005. Strategic N/NE borders. Snow clearance in high altitude.

nodes.label: NS-EW Corridors
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: NS: Srinagar-Kanyakumari 4,076 km with Kochi-Salem spur. EW: Silchar-Porbandar 3,640 km.

nodes.label: India Foreign Trade
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Grew from Rs.12,140M (1950-51) to Rs.8,37,1330M (2004-05). Imports exceed exports. Crude petroleum major import.

nodes.label: Trade Deficit
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Persistent negative balance. Increased due to crude petroleum prices. Strains financial reserves.

nodes.label: Water Pollution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Industries (leather, pulp, textiles, chemicals) main polluters. Ganga at Kanpur/Varanasi. Yamuna most polluted Delhi-Etawah. Agriculture chemicals infiltrate groundwater.

nodes.label: Air Pollution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fossil fuel combustion, mining, industries. SO2, NOx, CO, hydrocarbons, lead. Respiratory/nervous/circulatory diseases. Urban smog. Acid rain.

nodes.label: Noise Pollution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Measured in decibels. Factories, construction, automobiles, aircraft. Intensity declines with distance. Location-specific.

nodes.label: Urban Waste Disposal
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Metros 90% collected. Other cities 30-50% uncollected. Disease through flies/rodents. Resource for energy/compost.

nodes.label: Rural-Urban Migration Issues
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Poor bypass small cities for metros. Male-dominated. Low wages, family separation. Menial jobs in informal sector.

nodes.label: Problems of Slums
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Poor hygiene, no ventilation, no water/toilets. Dharavi Asia largest. Low-paid unorganised sector. Drug abuse, crime.

nodes.label: Land Degradation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Soil erosion, waterlogging, salinisation. 17.98% wasteland. Man-made 5.88%. NRSA classified via remote sensing.

nodes.label: Jhabua Watershed
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Backward tribal MP (Bhils). Govt-NGO partnership. Community participation. 20% area treated. CPR revitalisation.

nodes.label: Types of Pollution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Air, water, land, noise. Water Act 1974, Environment Protection Act 1986. CPCB monitors 507 stations.

nodes.label: Environmental Legislation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Water Act 1974, Environment Protection Act 1986, Water Cess Act 1977. Central/State Pollution Control Boards.

nodes.label: Rural-Urban Sex Ratio
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Western: males rural, females urban. Asian: reverse due to male urban migration. India: female participation high in rural farming.

nodes.label: The Sun
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: The nearest star to earth, about 150 million km away. Made of extremely hot gases. Ultimate source of heat and light for the solar system. Light takes about 8 minutes to reach earth from the sun.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: The Earth
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Third nearest planet to sun, fifth largest. Shape described as Geoid (slightly flattened at poles). Called the Blue Planet as two-thirds surface covered by water. Only planet with conditions supporting life: moderate temperature, water and oxygen-rich air.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: The Moon
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Earth's only natural satellite, about 3,84,400 km away. Diameter is one-quarter of earth's. Completes one revolution around earth in 27 days. Same side always faces earth. No water, no air. Neil Armstrong first stepped on it on 21 July 1969.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: Stars
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Celestial bodies made of hot gases with their own heat and light. The sun is the nearest star. Stars appear tiny due to enormous distance from earth. They appear to twinkle due to atmospheric refraction.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: Constellations
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Patterns formed by groups of stars in the night sky. Ursa Major (Big Bear) contains the Saptarishi group of seven stars. The Pole Star (North Star) always remains in the same position indicating north direction.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: Venus
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Considered Earth's twin because of similar size and shape. Second planet from the sun. One of the two planets that rotate clockwise (along with Uranus). Orbit around sun takes about 255 days.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: Milky Way Galaxy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: A huge system of billions of stars, dust and gases. Our solar system is part of it. Appears as a whitish broad band across the sky on clear nights. Called Akash Ganga in ancient India.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: Satellites
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Celestial bodies that move around planets. Can be natural (like the moon) or human-made (like INSAT, IRS, EDUSAT). Human-made satellites gather information about the universe and enable communication.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: Inner Planets
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Located close to the sun. Made up of rocks. Also called terrestrial or rocky planets. Relatively smaller in size compared to outer planets.
nodes.chapter_title: The Earth in the Solar System

nodes.label: North America
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Third largest continent. Linked to South America by Isthmus of Panama. Lies completely in Northern and Western Hemispheres. Surrounded by three oceans.

nodes.label: South America
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Mostly in Southern Hemisphere. Has the Andes, world's longest mountain range, and Amazon, world's largest river by volume. Connected to North America by Isthmus of Panama.

nodes.label: Antarctica
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Completely in Southern Hemisphere, permanently covered with thick ice. South Pole at its centre. No permanent human settlements. India has Maitri and Dakshin Gangotri research stations.

nodes.label: Plateaus
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Elevated flat-topped table land standing above surrounding area. Rich in mineral deposits. Deccan Plateau in India is one of the oldest. Tibet Plateau is the highest at 4000-6000m above sea level.

nodes.label: Aravali Hills
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: One of the oldest fold mountain systems in the world. Borders Peninsular Plateau on northwest side. Considerably worn down by erosion over time.

nodes.label: Thorny Bushes
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Found in dry areas. Leaves in form of spines to reduce water loss. Plants: cactus, khair, babool, keekar. Found in Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat, eastern slopes of Western Ghats.

nodes.label: Mangrove Forests
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Can survive in saline water. Found mainly in Sunderbans (West Bengal) and Andaman-Nicobar Islands. Sundari tree is a well-known species, after which Sunderbans are named.

nodes.label: National Parks and Sanctuaries
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Protected areas set up to conserve wildlife. Biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries protect habitats. Wildlife week observed in first week of October.

nodes.label: Migratory Birds
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Birds like Pintail Duck, Flamingo, Osprey migrate to India in winter. Smallest migratory bird Little Stint (15g) travels over 8000 km from Arctic region.

nodes.label: Biotic Components
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: The world of living organisms including plants and animals. Part of the biosphere. Interact with abiotic components to form ecosystems.

nodes.label: Abiotic Components
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: The world of non-living elements like land, water, air, minerals, climate. Provide the physical framework within which living organisms exist.

nodes.label: Biosphere Domain
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Narrow zone where land, water and air interact to support life. Plant and animal kingdoms together. Three domains of earth interact and affect each other.

nodes.label: Lithospheric Plates
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Earth's crust broken into large and small rigid irregular plates carrying continents and ocean floor. Move slowly (few mm per year) due to movement of molten magma inside earth.

nodes.label: Composition of Atmosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, other gases (CO2, helium, ozone, argon, hydrogen) 1%. CO2 creates greenhouse effect trapping heat. Increase in CO2 causes global warming.

nodes.label: Spring Tides
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Highest tides occurring during full moon and new moon when sun, moon and earth are aligned. Gravitational pulls of sun and moon combine.

nodes.label: Neap Tides
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Low tides during first and last quarter of moon when sun and moon are at right angles. Ocean waters drawn in diagonally opposite directions.

nodes.label: Deforestation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Clearing of forests for agriculture, settlements and timber. Leads to soil erosion, loss of biodiversity, climate change. Natural vegetation destroyed at large scale worldwide.

nodes.label: Roadways
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Most common transport for short distances. Metalled (pucca) and unmetalled (kutcha). Manali-Leh highway among highest in world. Subways built underground, flyovers on raised structures. Golden Quadrilateral connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment: Settlement, Transport and Communication

nodes.label: Railways
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Carry heavy goods and people over long distances quickly and cheaply. Indian railway network largest in Asia. Trans-Siberian Railway longest system connecting St Petersburg to Vladivostok.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment: Settlement, Transport and Communication

nodes.label: Waterways
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Cheapest for carrying heavy bulky goods over long distances. Inland waterways (Ganga-Brahmaputra, Great Lakes, Nile) and sea routes. Important ports: Singapore, Mumbai, New York, London.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment: Settlement, Transport and Communication

nodes.label: Airways
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fastest but most expensive transport. Developed in early 20th century. Only mode to reach most remote areas. Adversely affected by fog and storms. Helicopters useful in calamities.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment: Settlement, Transport and Communication

nodes.label: Trans-Siberian Railway
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Longest railway system in the world connecting St Petersburg in western Russia to Vladivostok on Pacific coast. Crosses multiple time zones.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment: Settlement, Transport and Communication

nodes.label: Amazon Basin
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Largest river basin in the world, in equatorial region (10N-10S) of South America. Hot and wet climate year-round. Drains parts of Brazil, Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment Interactions: Tropical and Subtropical Region

nodes.label: Amazon Rainforest
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Dense tropical rainforest in Amazon Basin. Canopy so thick sunlight cannot reach ground. Rich fauna: toucans, humming birds, monkeys, sloth, tapirs, anaconda, piranha fish. Called lungs of earth.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment Interactions: Tropical and Subtropical Region

nodes.label: Slash and Burn Agriculture
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Farming method where forest is cleared by cutting and burning trees. Ashes mixed with soil for nutrients. After fertility declines, land abandoned for new plot. Called Jhumming in NE India, Milpa in Mexico, Roca in Brazil.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment Interactions: Tropical and Subtropical Region

nodes.label: Ganga-Brahmaputra Basin
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: River basin in Indian subcontinent between 10N-30N latitudes. Monsoon climate. Main features: Ganga-Brahmaputra plains, Himalayan foothills, Sundarbans delta. Very high population density.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment Interactions: Tropical and Subtropical Region

nodes.label: Ganga Basin Vegetation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Plains have tropical deciduous trees (teak, sal, peepal). Thick bamboo in Brahmaputra plain. Delta covered with mangrove forests. Mountains have coniferous trees (pine, deodar, fir).
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment Interactions: Tropical and Subtropical Region

nodes.label: Ganga Basin Wildlife
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Elephants, tigers, deer, monkeys. One-horned rhinoceros in Brahmaputra plain. Bengal tiger and crocodiles in delta. Susu (blind dolphin) in fresh waters - indicator of river health.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment Interactions: Tropical and Subtropical Region

nodes.label: Trans-Amazon Highway
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Built in 1970, made all parts of Amazon rainforest accessible. Led to displacement of indigenous population and gradual destruction of biologically diverse rainforests.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment Interactions: Tropical and Subtropical Region

nodes.label: Kaziranga Wildlife Sanctuary
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Located in Assam in the Ganga-Brahmaputra basin. Home to one-horned rhinoceros. Important tourist attraction along with Manas wildlife sanctuary in Arunachal Pradesh.
nodes.chapter_title: Human Environment Interactions: Tropical and Subtropical Region

nodes.label: Resource Conservation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Using resources carefully and giving them time to renew. Reducing consumption, recycling and reusing. Even renewable resources can become scarce through overuse and pollution.

nodes.label: Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Plants provide timber, shelter, oxygen, protect soil, give fruits, nuts, medicine, paper. Wildlife provides milk, meat, hides, wool. Bees provide honey and pollination. Vultures are vital scavengers.
nodes.chapter_title: Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources

nodes.label: Biosphere Reserves
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Series of protected areas linked through global network. Demonstrate relationship between conservation and development. Along with national parks and sanctuaries, protect natural vegetation and wildlife.
nodes.chapter_title: Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources

nodes.label: Poaching and Wildlife Trade
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Sharp decline in species due to illegal hunting and trade in hides, skins, nails, teeth, horns, feathers. Affected species: tiger, lion, elephant, deer, rhinoceros, snow leopard, peacock. Many countries have passed laws against it.
nodes.chapter_title: Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources

nodes.label: Geothermal Energy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Heat from earth's interior surfacing as hot springs. Used for cooking, heating, power generation. USA has largest plants. India: Manikaran (HP), Puga Valley (Ladakh).

nodes.label: Biogas
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: From decomposition of organic waste (dead plant/animal material, dung, kitchen waste) by bacteria. Mixture of methane and CO2. Excellent fuel for cooking and lighting, produces organic manure.

nodes.label: Conventional Energy Sources
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Sources in common use for long time: firewood and fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas). Over 50% village energy from firewood. Fossil fuels depleting at alarming rate and cause pollution.

nodes.label: Industry
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Economic activity concerned with production of goods, extraction of minerals or provision of services. Classified by raw materials (agro/mineral/marine/forest based), size (cottage/small/large), ownership (private/public/joint/cooperative).

nodes.label: Factors of Industrial Location
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Availability of raw materials, land, water, labour, power, capital, transport and market. Government incentives for backward areas. Industrialisation leads to urban growth.

nodes.label: Cooperative Sector Industries
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Owned and operated by producers/suppliers of raw materials or workers. Anand Milk Union Limited (Amul) and Sudha Dairy are successful cooperatives.

nodes.label: Bhopal Gas Tragedy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Worst industrial disaster. 3 December 1984, MIC gas leaked from Union Carbide pesticide factory. Official death toll 3598 in 1989. Thousands still suffer from ailments. Highlighted need for industrial safety.

nodes.label: Population Change
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Due to births, deaths and migration. Natural growth rate = birth rate minus death rate. World reached 1 billion in 1804, 3 billion in 1959, 6 billion in 1999. Population explosion due to better food and medicine reducing deaths while births remain high.

nodes.label: Birth Rate and Death Rate
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Birth rate: live births per 1000 people. Death rate: deaths per 1000 people. When birth rate exceeds death rate, population increases. Better healthcare reduced death rates globally.

nodes.label: Migration
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Movement of people in and out of areas. Emigrants leave a country, immigrants arrive. General trend: less developed to more developed nations for employment. Rural to urban within countries for jobs, education, health.

nodes.label: Population Pyramid
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Graphical representation of age-sex composition. Broad base with narrow top: high births and deaths (Kenya). Broad in younger groups: decreasing child mortality (India). Narrow base: low birth rate, ageing population (Japan).

nodes.label: The Northern Plains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Formed by alluvial deposits of Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra. About 2400 km long, 240-320 km wide. Divided into Punjab Plains (Indus), Ganga Plains, Brahmaputra Plain. Three zones: bhabar, tarai, alluvial plains (bangar-old, khadar-new).

nodes.label: Bhabar, Tarai and Alluvial Plains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Bhabar: narrow pebble belt at foothills, 8-16 km wide, streams disappear. Tarai: marshy, wet belt south of bhabar, rich in wildlife. Alluvial plains: older alluvium (bangar) has calcareous deposits (kankar), newer alluvium (khadar) refreshed by floods.

nodes.label: Deccan Plateau
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Triangular landmass south of Narmada. Higher in west, slopes gently east. Western Ghats (Sahyadri) on west, Eastern Ghats on east. Anai Mudi (2695m) highest peak in Western Ghats, Dodda Betta (2637m) in Nilgiris.

nodes.label: Eastern Ghats
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Discontinuous, broken by rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri). Lower than Western Ghats, average 600m. Highest: Mahendragiri (1501m). Merge with Western Ghats in Nilgiri hills.

nodes.label: The Indian Desert
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: West of Aravali hills. Sandy, arid climate with very low rainfall below 150mm/year. Luni is the only large river. Crescent-shaped sand dunes (barchans). Characterized by low vegetation.

nodes.label: Western Coastal Plains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Narrow strip between Western Ghats and Arabian Sea. From Gujarat to Kerala. Three parts: Konkan (Mumbai-Goa), Kanara (Karnataka), Malabar coast (Kerala). Natural harbours for ports.

nodes.label: Eastern Coastal Plains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Wider plain along Bay of Bengal. Two parts: Northern Circar (north) and Coromandel coast (south). Rivers form large deltas: Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri. Chilika Lake is largest brackish water lagoon.

nodes.label: Indus River System
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Originates near Mansarovar lake in Tibet. Total length 2900 km (India: 1114 km). Tributaries: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej (Panj-nad). Indus Waters Treaty 1960 between India and Pakistan.

nodes.label: Ganga River System
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Originates at Gangotri glacier as Bhagirathi. Joined by Alaknanda at Devprayag becoming Ganga. Length about 2500 km. Tributaries: Yamuna, Ghaghra, Gandak, Kosi (left); Son, Chambal (right). Largest basin in India.

nodes.label: Brahmaputra River System
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Originates east of Mansarovar as Tsangpo in Tibet. Enters India through Arunachal Pradesh as Dihang. Tributaries: Subansiri, Dibang, Lohit. Carries enormous sediment, forms large islands (Majuli). Floods frequently in Assam.

nodes.label: Krishna River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Originates near Mahabaleshwar. Tributaries: Tungabhadra, Koyna, Ghatprabha, Musi, Bhima. Second largest Peninsular river. Drains parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, AP.

nodes.label: Kaveri River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Originates at Talakaveri on Brahmagiri range in Coorg (Karnataka). Tributaries: Amravati, Bhavani, Hemavati, Kabini. Known as Ganga of the South. Water dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

nodes.label: Narmada River
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Originates from Amarkantak in MP. Flows westward through a rift valley between Vindhya and Satpura. Falls into Arabian Sea via Gujarat. Forms many waterfalls (Dhuadhar Falls at Jabalpur). No delta, forms estuary.

nodes.label: Drainage Patterns
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Dendritic (tree-like, most common), trellis (parallel tributaries join at right angles), rectangular (right-angle bends), radial (rivers flow from central peak in all directions like spokes).

nodes.label: SW Monsoon Branches
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Arabian Sea branch: strikes Western Ghats causing heavy orographic rain on windward side. Bay of Bengal branch: moves along Ganga valley. Arrival called 'burst' of monsoon. Enters India around June 1 in Kerala.

nodes.label: Retreating Monsoon
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: October-November. Monsoon withdraws from NW India by early September, from rest by mid-October. Clear skies and rising temperatures (October Heat). NE monsoon brings rain to Tamil Nadu from Bay of Bengal.

nodes.label: Cold Weather Season (Winter)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: December to February. NE trade winds prevail. Low temperatures in north, mild in south. Western disturbances from Mediterranean bring winter rain to NW India (important for rabi crops). Chennai gets rain from NE monsoon.

nodes.label: October Heat
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Period during retreating monsoon with high temperatures and humidity. Land still moist, creating oppressive conditions. Clear skies during day, cool nights.

nodes.label: Wildlife Protection Act
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Enacted in 1972 to protect wildlife and their habitats. Provides for national parks, sanctuaries and closed areas. Bans hunting. Indian Board for Wildlife advises government on policy.

nodes.label: Conservation Movements
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Chipko Movement (1974, Uttarakhand): people hugged trees to prevent logging. Joint Forest Management (JFM) involves local communities. Conservation requires both government action and community participation.

nodes.label: India's Population Growth
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Slow growth till 1921 (stagnant), steady increase 1921-1951, rapid acceleration 1951-1981 (population explosion), declining growth rate since 1981. Annual growth rate 1.64% (2001-2011). Added 181 million in 2001-2011.
